newsitem.title: USA: Stakes higher for US/Japan trade data after Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Stakes higher for US/Japan trade data after Rubin.

text.p: Import/export data from Japan and the United States this week will be scrutinized to confirm if the dollar's rally and yen's tumble have derailed last year's improvement in bilateral trade balances, international economists said.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin's recent expression of concern about the impact of a falling yen on Japan's external trade surplus has placed trade data from Japan and the U.S. squarely in the currency markets' sights.
Trade data from both nations are due on Thursday.
"If the trade numbers are bad it's just going to focus more attention on the strong dollar," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman of Goldman, Sachs (International).

The Treasury chief has repeatedly said exchange rates were not on the table as a tool to manage trade policy. But currency experts said if the repairs to trade relations in 1996 come unstitched in coming months, it could increasingly have a bearing on the dollar.
Recent data from both countries suggest that falling Japanese trade surpluses and narrower U.S. trade deficits, especially with Japan in 1996, have reversed course.

Although Rubin supported Japan's efforts to deregulate and stimulate its domestic economy during his recent visit to Tokyo, one of his main objectives was to block Japan's external surplus from growing again as a proportion of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), experts said.
"I think the stakes are up a bit," said David Gilmore, a partner at consulting firm Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"To put it in perspective the (trade surplus) situation is vastly improved from where it was. The worry is: Is it going back to the 3.0-percent level," Gilmore asked.

"(Rubin) wants to be sure (Japanese) exports are not the driver of growth -- that the driver of growth is domestic demand, and if exports start rising as a percentage of GDP, it does mean they are a driver of growth," Hormats said.
Chris Widness, an international economist at Chase Securities Inc, said Rubin recently seemed to imply that as long as Japan's surplus stayed at 1.5 to 2.0 percent of GDP, it would not be a problem.
But Japan's surplus started to blow out around November and reached a level that suggested it was going above 2.0 percent, he said.
"So I think the market is still attuned to watching the trends on Japan's trade, and Rubin has given them a trial period of watching and waiting," Widness added.

Data on Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus for March is due for relase on Thursday. Widness said he expects the surplus to come in between 800 and 880 billion yen, down from 1.13 trillion yen in March 1996.
The U.S. trade gap for February, meanwhile, was expected on average to have been $10.1 billion, down from a shocking $12.71 billion gap in January, its highest in nearly a decade.
But Widness said seasonal adjustment problems tend to depress the U.S. trade deficit in the first quarter and Thursday's data could reflect this seasonal factor.
The Clinton administration, it seems, is now in a rock-and-a-hard-place-type bind.

Rubin is stuck not wanting to weaken the dollar for fear of hurting the U.S. Treasury bond market, which would push up U.S. interest rates, while grasping for a vehicle to let Japan know he is serious about it containing the trade surplus, economists said.
"The more Japan resists and the more (Washington) complains about trade imbalances, the only place where the adjustment can take place is on the currency," Gilmore said.
"If they freeze it via intervention or jawboning; if they manage it in a range, then the outcome is what they don't want -- a wider trade gap," he added.

"We could be heading to this 'deja-vu all over again' with the U.S. and Japan, where Japan is trying to ride a weak yen to export-led recovery and the U.S. is increasingly angry about it," concluded Josh Feinman, global markets economist at Bankers Trust Co.
